findings.remediation: Add an authentication check to the policy: USING (auth.uid() = user_id) or WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = user_id)

findings.description: RLS is enabled but FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is not set. Table owners bypass RLS by default unless FORCE is enabled.
findings.remediation: Add FORCE RLS: ALTER TABLE table_name FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; This ensures even the table owner respects RLS policies.

context.issue: RLS enabled but FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY not set

findings.rule_name: UPDATE policy missing WITH CHECK clause
findings.description: UPDATE policy has USING but no WITH CHECK. Users may update rows to values that violate the policy.
findings.remediation: Add WITH CHECK clause: USING (condition) WITH CHECK (condition) to ensure updated rows comply with policy

findings.rule_name: Policy uses IN with subquery joining source table
findings.description: Policy uses IN with a subquery that joins to the source table. This causes performance issues.
findings.remediation: Rewrite to avoid join: col IN (SELECT col FROM table WHERE user_id = auth.uid()) instead of auth.uid() IN (SELECT user_id FROM table WHERE table.col = source.col)

findings.description: Policy uses FOR ALL which applies to all operations. This may be too broad for security requirements.
findings.remediation: Consider creating separate policies for each operation (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) for more granular control.

context.reason: FOR ALL without auth checks or public data justification
